the first law of black hole thermodynamics is satisfied for non-extremal D-brane probes in non-extremally charged Dp-brane backgrounds and in near-horizon AdS backgrounds, and that the same holds for extremal probes in extremal backgrounds.
the entropy of the probe is equal to that of the black hole.
the thermodynamics of BPS probes is consistent with that of a black hole and that this is a quantitative indicator of thermalization in gauge theories.

the thermodynamic properties of D-brane and string probes moving in nonextremal black hole backgrounds, in particular, the entropy of the probe as it reaches the horizon.
understanding the thermodynamics of non-extremal brane probes, and the relation to gauge theory.
the thermodynamics and dynamics of particle and brane probes in non-extremally charged black hole/brane geometries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the entropy of non-extremal branes is given by the Bekenstein-Hawking formula, and the entropy of extremal branes is the Bekenstein entropy plus a contribution from the gauge theory.
in the extremal limit, the entropy is proportional to the number of degrees of freedom in the gauge theory, while in the Schwarzschild case it is proportional to the area of the event horizon.
the entropy is the number of microstates in the gauge theory.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in a non-extremal background, a probe moving from infinity to the horizon is thermalized and the heat absorbed by the black-hole is the entropy change of the probe.
the thermodynamic relation TdS is valid not just in the near-hormizon limit, but also in the far-horizon limit (asymptotically flat space) for BPS branes.
the thermodynamic relation between the probe and the background black hole is the same in the near-horzion limit and in the asymptotic region, for BPS particles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the thermodynamics of probes in the near-hornizon geometry is a powerful tool to study the thermodynamics of the full black hole/brane background.
the thermodynamics of the probe can be used to extract the entropy of the black hole.
the first law of brane thermodynamics can be used to reliably determine the entropy of a black hole/brane background in the non-extremal regime.
